slides.title: SOLID Principles in Python
slides.prompt: SOLID principles guide robust, maintainable enterprise software design: Single Responsibility (SRP), Open/Closed (OCP), Liskov Substitution (LSP), Interface Segregation (ISP), and Dependency Inversion (DIP).

slides.title: Open/Closed Principle Definition
slides.prompt: Software entities should be open for extension, but closed for ___.
options: modification
deletion
inheritance
instantiation

slides.title: Liskov Substitution Principle Violation
slides.prompt: Which scenario clearly violates the Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)?
options: A subclass overrides a parent method and throws an unexpected exception for valid parent inputs
A subclass adds a new method not present in the parent class
A class implements multiple abstract interfaces
A subclass calls `super().__init__()` in its constructor
slides.correctAnswer: A subclass overrides a parent method and throws an unexpected exception for valid parent inputs

slides.title: Single Responsibility Principle Focus
slides.prompt: Fill in the missing word: A class should have one, and only one, reason to ___.
options: change
execute
fail
inherit

slides.title: Interface Segregation in Python
slides.prompt: How is the Interface Segregation Principle (ISP) implemented in Python using Abstract Base Classes?
options: By creating small, specific ABC interfaces rather than one large multi-purpose interface
By placing all abstract methods in a single monolithic parent class
By using private variables prefixed with double underscores
By avoiding the use of inheritance altogether
slides.correctAnswer: By creating small, specific ABC interfaces rather than one large multi-purpose interface

slides.title: Dependency Inversion Abstraction Rule
slides.prompt: Fill in the missing word: High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules. Both should depend on ___.
slides.codeSnippet:
# High-level and low-level modules depend on ___
from abc import ABC
options: abstractions
concrete classes
global variables
C-extensions

slides.title: Dependency Injection Benefit
slides.prompt: What is the primary architectural benefit of using Dependency Injection (DI)?
options: It decouples components, making unit testing and swapping implementations easy
It speeds up execution time by pre-compiling Python bytecode to C
It eliminates the need for garbage collection in long-running processes
It enforces single-threaded execution across multi-core processors
slides.correctAnswer: It decouples components, making unit testing and swapping implementations easy
